canonical_statement: Perform an A1C test on all people with diabetes or hyperglycemia (random blood glucose >140 mg/dL [>7.8 mmol/L]) at hospital admission if no A1C result is available from the prior 3 months.
Institutions should use validated written or computerized provider order entry protocols for inpatient dysglycemia that allow a personalized approach.
When caring for hospitalized people with diabetes or stress hyperglycemia, consult a specialized diabetes or glucose management team when available.
For most critically ill adults, initiate or intensify insulin for persistent hyperglycemia at ≥180 mg/dL (≥10.0 mmol/L) confirmed twice within 24 hours.
For most noncritically ill adults, initiate or intensify insulin and/or other glucose-lowering therapy for persistent hyperglycemia at ≥180 mg/dL (≥10.0 mmol/L) confirmed twice within 24 hours.

Once therapy is initiated, target 140–180 mg/dL (7.8–10.0 mmol/L) for most critically ill adults; selected critically ill adults may use more stringent individualized goals if achievable without significant hypoglycemia.
For noncritically ill adults, target 100–180 mg/dL (5.6–10.0 mmol/L) if achievable without significant hypoglycemia.

Continue a personal CGM during hospitalization when clinically appropriate, with confirmatory POC glucose for insulin dosing and hypoglycemia assessment, when resources, training, and an institutional protocol are available.

Continue insulin pump use, including automated insulin delivery, during hospitalization when clinically appropriate and when supplies, resources, training, competency assessment, and institutional technology protocols are available.
Use continuous intravenous insulin infusion to achieve glycemic goals and avoid hypoglycemia in critically ill adults.
For noncritically ill hospitalized adults with poor or no oral intake, basal insulin or basal plus correction insulin is preferred.
For most noncritically ill hospitalized adults with adequate nutritional intake, use an insulin plan with basal, prandial, and correction components.
For most hospitalized adults, sole use of correction or supplemental insulin without basal insulin is discouraged.
Initiate or continue an SGLT2 inhibitor during hospitalization when indicated for heart failure and no contraindication is present.

Health systems should adopt a hypoglycemia management protocol, establish an individualized identification/treatment/prevention plan, and document and track hospital hypoglycemia for quality improvement.
When blood glucose <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L) is documented, review and change the treatment plan as needed to prevent hypoglycemia and recurrence.
For elective surgery, recommend a preoperative A1C <8% (<64 mmol/mol) within 3 months after individualized risk-benefit assessment; 14-day GMI <8% and/or time in range >50% may also be used.
Monitor blood glucose before, during, and after surgery and generally maintain 100–180 mg/dL (5.6–10.0 mmol/L), individualized for surgery, hypoglycemia risk, and therapy.
Manage DKA and HHS with intravenous fluids, insulin, and electrolytes; monitor closely; bridge promptly to maintenance subcutaneous insulin; and identify and treat the precipitating cause.
Discharge planning for people affected by or at high risk for DKA/HHS should include education on recognition, prevention, and management to reduce recurrence and readmission.
Tailor a structured discharge plan to the individual with diabetes and, when discharge is not to home, consider the receiving facility’s diabetes-management capabilities.
In hospitalized people, hyperglycemia, hypoglycemia, and glucose variability are associated with increased morbidity and mortality.
An admission A1C ≥6.5% (≥48 mmol/mol) suggests diabetes preceded hospitalization.
A virtual glucose management service based on daily chart review and EHR recommendations reduced hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia rates by 30–40% versus usual care in a cross-sectional study.
Hospital hyperglycemia is defined as blood glucose >140 mg/dL (>7.8 mmol/L).

outcome.definition: Blood glucose <70 mg/dL; level 1 54–69 mg/dL; level 2 <54 mg/dL; level 3 event requiring assistance

canonical_statement: Hospital hypoglycemia is blood glucose <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L), with level 1 at 54–69 mg/dL, level 2 <54 mg/dL, and level 3 requiring assistance because of altered mental and/or physical functioning.

population.label: Critically ill hospitalized people in NICE-SUGAR

canonical_statement: In NICE-SUGAR, mortality was 27.5% with intensive glycemic management (80–110 mg/dL) versus 25.0% with moderate goals (140–180 mg/dL), an absolute difference of 2.5 percentage points calculated from the chapter’s reported rates.
The intensive NICE-SUGAR group had 10- to 15-fold greater rates of hypoglycemia than the moderate-goal group.
A recent multicenter ICU trial reported hypoglycemia rates of 1.0% with tight glucose management and 0.7% with liberal management, with no benefit from tight management.
Fasting glucose <100 mg/dL (<5.6 mmol/L) predicts hypoglycemia within the next 24 hours and may require basal insulin dose adjustment.
For hospitalized people who are eating, POC glucose should be checked before meals; when not eating, every 4–6 hours; intravenous insulin generally requires checks every 30 minutes to 2 hours.
The chapter’s modified 20/20 CGM validation criterion requires CGM within ±20% of POC when glucose is ≥70 mg/dL or within ±20 mg/dL when glucose is <70 mg/dL.
At publication, no CGM device was FDA-approved for inpatient use.

population.label: People with type 2 diabetes hospitalized for noncritical illness in a multicenter randomized trial

canonical_statement: A multicenter noncritical-care trial reported mean blood glucose 170 mg/dL with CGM versus 175 mg/dL with POC monitoring (P=0.25), a calculated mean difference of -5 mg/dL.
Inpatient hybrid closed-loop/AID evidence remains limited, including feasibility trials, and best-practice policies are still evolving.
A hospital survey found fewer than half of hospitals had institutional policies for inpatient diabetes technology in place.
When stopping an intravenous insulin infusion, give subcutaneous basal insulin about 2 hours before discontinuation to minimize rebound hyperglycemia.
Low-dose basal insulin analog (0.15–0.3 units/kg) added to IV insulin may shorten infusion duration and hospital stay and prevent rebound hyperglycemia without increasing hypoglycemia.
A usual starting inpatient total daily insulin dose is 0.3–0.6 units/kg/day, individualized to insulin sensitivity.

The chapter describes estimating inpatient total daily insulin as 80% of the home dose or from recent IV infusion needs; when calculated from infusion rate, about 60% may be used, then approximately half as basal and half as nutritional insulin.
For hospitalized people with type 1 diabetes, correctional insulin alone is contraindicated; basal insulin is required even when NPO.
People using U-500 insulin may have inpatient insulin requirements reduced by up to 75% versus home dosing; concentrated insulin requires safeguards against dosing errors.
A randomized inpatient trial found 70/30 NPH/regular premix and basal-bolus had comparable glycemic outcomes but significantly more hypoglycemia with premix.

DPP-4 inhibitors with or without basal insulin may offer a simpler, lower-hypoglycemia approach for selected hospitalized people with mild-to-moderate hyperglycemia, such as admission glucose <180–200 mg/dL.
Inpatient GLP-1 receptor agonist data are mostly limited to research studies and medically stable selected populations; the chapter says to hold GLP-1 RAs in acutely ill hospitalized people.
Bundled inpatient hypoglycemia-prevention programs reduced hypoglycemic events by 56–80% versus baseline in cited studies.
Treat hospital hypoglycemia with 15 g fast-acting carbohydrate when safe to swallow and not NPO, or IV glucose/glucagon; recheck every 15 minutes and repeat until glucose is above 70 mg/dL.
In one hospital study, 84% of people with severe hypoglycemia <40 mg/dL had a preceding episode <70 mg/dL during the same admission.
In another hospital study of glucose <50 mg/dL, 78% were receiving basal insulin and events peaked from midnight to 6 A.M.; 75% did not have the basal dose changed before the next administration.
Kidney failure is an important inpatient hypoglycemia risk factor, with advanced age, heart/liver failure, sepsis, and malnutrition also identified as related risks.

Hospital nutrition should be individualized; controlled-carbohydrate meal plans can facilitate matching prandial insulin to carbohydrate, and glucose checks, meal delivery, and nutritional insulin should be coordinated as a “meal triad.”

Inpatient diabetes self-management may be appropriate for selected people who successfully self-manage at home, retain cognitive and physical skills, have adequate oral intake, and have stable insulin requirements.

For enteral/parenteral nutrition requiring insulin, orders should cover basal, prandial/nutritional, and correction needs, and people with type 1 diabetes must continue basal insulin even if feeding stops.
For enteral/parenteral carbohydrate coverage, the chapter describes approximately 1 unit insulin per 10–15 g carbohydrate, with regimen timing matched to feeding mode.

For continuous parenteral nutrition, regular insulin may be added to the nutrition solution, especially if >20 units correction insulin were needed in the prior 24 hours; a starting ratio of 1 unit per 10 g dextrose is described.
Continuous enteral/parenteral nutrition produces a continuous postprandial state; attempting glucose <140 mg/dL substantially increases hypoglycemia risk.
Consistent glucocorticoid use occurs in about 10–15% of hospitalized people and can induce hyperglycemia in 56–86% with or without preexisting diabetes.
For prednisone/prednisolone, NPH timed with steroid dosing is a common approach; with higher glucocorticoid doses, prandial/correction insulin may need increases of 40–60% or more.
Up to 20% of people undergoing major general surgery have diabetes and 23–60% have prediabetes or undiagnosed diabetes, according to the chapter’s cited estimates.
Because interventional data are lacking, the chapter says elective surgery should not be postponed based on A1C or GMI alone.
While NPO perioperatively, check blood glucose at least every 2–4 hours; insulin is the recommended glucose-lowering medication, and CGM should not be used alone during surgery.

For many surgical patients, the chapter describes reducing the preceding evening basal insulin by about 25%, NPH to one-half, or long-acting basal analogs to 75–80%, individualized especially in type 1 diabetes.
SGLT2 inhibitors should be held 3–4 days before elective surgery, with nonelective surgery requiring monitoring for DKA including euglycemic DKA.

population.label: People with type 2 diabetes requiring emergency surgery in a retrospective study

quantitative_result.effect_measure: unadjusted absolute DKA risk difference, percentage points
quantitative_result.original_result_text: incidence of DKA was 4.9% ... and 3.5% ... After adjustment ... not statistically significant

canonical_statement: In a retrospective emergency-surgery study, DKA occurred in 4.9% of SGLT2 inhibitor users versus 3.5% of nonusers; the calculated raw absolute difference was 1.4 percentage points, while the chapter reports the adjusted difference was not statistically significant.

For GLP-1–based therapies, the chapter notes insufficient information on mitigating perioperative aspiration risk and an unknown withholding duration; one retrospective study found increased residual gastric content despite semaglutide withholding up to 30 days (average 10 days).

Perioperative GLP-1/GIP-GLP-1 management should be personalized based on indication, glycemic control, dose/duration, gastrointestinal symptoms, procedure urgency/type, and anesthesia; options include gastric ultrasound, full-stomach precautions, or a 24-hour liquid nutrition protocol in higher-risk situations.
Approximately 1% of hospitalizations among people with diabetes are for hyperglycemic crises, and about 10% of DKA presents as euglycemic DKA with plasma glucose <200 mg/dL.
Recent hyperglycemic-crisis rates cited by the chapter reach 44.5–82.6 per 1,000 person-years in type 1 diabetes and up to 3.2 per 1,000 person-years in type 2 diabetes.
Recent inpatient DKA mortality cited by the chapter ranges from 0.2% in type 1 diabetes to 1.0% in type 2 diabetes.

population.label: People with type 2 diabetes hospitalized for HHS

canonical_statement: Among hospitalized people with type 2 diabetes and HHS, inpatient mortality decreased from 1.44% in 2008 to 0.77% in 2018, a calculated absolute change of -0.67 percentage points.
After a DKA hospitalization, the chapter reports a 1-year age-corrected mortality rate 13 times that of the general population.

DKA diagnostic criteria require diabetes/hyperglycemia (glucose ≥200 mg/dL or prior diabetes), ketosis (β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L or urine ketones ≥2+), and metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L).

HHS diagnostic criteria require plasma glucose ≥600 mg/dL, hyperosmolarity (effective >300 mOsm/kg or total >320 mOsm/kg), β-hydroxybutyrate <3.0 mmol/L or urine ketones <2+, pH ≥7.3, and bicarbonate ≥15 mmol/L.
Table 16.2 states that one-third of hyperglycemic emergencies have a hybrid DKA-HHS presentation.
Figure 16.1 directs frequent DKA/HHS monitoring of electrolytes, kidney function, venous pH, osmolality, and glucose every 2–4 hours until stable.
Figure 16.1 recommends adding 5% or 10% dextrose when glucose falls below 250 mg/dL; in euglycemic DKA, dextrose is started alongside crystalloid at initiation of insulin treatment.

Figure 16.1 uses IV insulin 0.1 units/kg/h for moderate/severe DKA, IV insulin 0.05 units/kg/h for HHS, and subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin 0.1 units/kg hourly or 0.2 units/kg every 2 hours for mild DKA.

Figure 16.1 recommends potassium replacement of 10–20 mmol/L/h when K+ <3.5 mmol/L until >3.5; when K+ is 3.5–5.0, add 10–20 mmol/L to each liter as needed to maintain 4–5; when K+ >5.0, start insulin without potassium and recheck every 2 hours.

Figure 16.1 defines DKA resolution as venous pH >7.3 or bicarbonate >18 mmol/L plus plasma/capillary ketones <0.6 mmol/L; HHS resolution includes osmolality <300 mOsm/kg, urine output >0.5 mL/kg/h, and glucose <250 mg/dL.

Figure 16.1 states bicarbonate should be considered only if pH <7.0 and phosphate should not be given unless muscle weakness/respiratory compromise is present with phosphate <1.0 mmol/L or <0.32 mmol/L.
For severe DKA/HHS, the chapter uses continuous IV insulin; transition to subcutaneous insulin requires basal insulin 2–4 hours before stopping IV insulin.
Mild uncomplicated DKA can be managed with subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin every 1–2 hours in an emergency department or step-down unit, with adequate fluid replacement and frequent monitoring.
Several studies found bicarbonate did not change DKA acidosis resolution or time to discharge, so routine use is generally not recommended.
A structured individualized discharge plan may reduce hospital length of stay and readmission and increase satisfaction; discharge planning should begin at admission and evolve as needs change.

After inpatient hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia, outpatient follow-up within 1 month is advised; if medications change or glycemic management is not optimal at discharge, follow-up in 1–2 weeks is preferred.
At minimum, discharge plans should include medication reconciliation, structured discharge communication, and diabetes education.
Hospital readmission among people with diabetes is 14–20%, nearly twice the rate in people without diabetes.
Among hospitalized people with diabetes, 30% have two or more days of hospital stays, and those admissions account for over 50% of hospital costs for diabetes.
The chapter states there is no standardized protocol to prevent diabetes-related hospital readmissions, although several successful strategies have been reported.
The chapter anticipates EHR decision support, diabetes devices, and dosing algorithms will continue changing inpatient diabetes care and care transitions.
